sections.title: Acknowledgements
sections.text:
Writing a short book still takes a crowd, and I'd like to thank the people who made room for this one.

First, my family. You put up with the notebook on the kitchen table, the half-finished sentences at dinner and the evenings I disappeared to write. You never made me feel I was wasting my time, and you were honest when an idea needed to be thrown away. That honesty shaped the whole method in these pages.

Thank you to my friends and to the colleagues I've worked alongside over the years. Many of you have asked me, in passing, whether a small idea of yours might be worth trying. Those conversations are why I wanted a plain, steady way to answer. You also reminded me how little spare time most of us have, which is why this book is short and the steps are small.

Thank you to the early readers who gave their time to the draft. You told me where I was being vague, where a term needed explaining and where I sounded more sure than I had any right to be. Every one of those comments made the book fairer and clearer for you, the next reader.

I'm grateful too to the people who share what they know freely, in community groups, forums and reviews. Much of the method depends on listening to what real people say they need, and they say it generously.

Last, thank you. You have a day job, a limited budget and probably an idea that keeps nagging at you. You chose to test it carefully rather than rush. Whatever you decide in the end, whether that's go, change or stop, you've taken the sensible first step. I hope this book saves you some time and money, and I'd be glad to hear how it goes.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text:
It's a weeknight, a little after nine. You're at the kitchen table with a notebook, a cup of tea going cold beside it, and a page that's still blank. (This scene is illustrative, but you may know it well.) Earlier you scrolled past three videos of people cheerfully explaining how they'd used AI to start something on the side. You felt, as you often do, that everyone else had been handed a map and you'd missed the post.

You haven't missed anything. You have a day job, a few spare hours and a small budget. You'd like to find out whether an idea of yours is worth the effort, without losing money on it or feeling foolish. That's a reasonable thing to want, and it's what this book is for.

Here's the honest version. An AI tool will not build a business for you, and anyone who says otherwise is usually selling something. What it can do is make the slow, fiddly parts of testing a small idea quicker. It can help you brainstorm, draft a sample and tidy a page of text. The judgement stays with you. So does the checking, and so does the asking of real people what they'd actually pay for.

I should say plainly where I'm coming from. I have no credentials to wave at you. I'm not a business school graduate, a famous founder or a technology insider, and I won't pretend to be. I wrote this because so much of the noise around AI is about tools, and tools change every few weeks. What lasts is a method: pick a problem, test it cheaply, price it fairly and make a decision. I've kept it short and plain, so a complete beginner can follow it.

The path is three chapters long. The first helps you choose one idea. You'll list what you already know and do well, use a free chat assistant to suggest ten ideas, and throw most of them away. (A chat assistant is a program you type questions to and it writes back. A free plan is the no-cost version of a tool, usually with limits.) Then you'll look for signs that real people are already asking for help, and write your idea on a single card.

The second chapter shows you how to test that idea before you build anything. You'll set a monthly spending cap of your own and write it down before you sign up for anything. You'll read the terms of any free plan before you sell what it produces, because some limit commercial use, which simply means using the output to earn money. Then you'll make one sample, write one plain page and have five honest conversations.

The third chapter is about the price and the decision. You'll learn to charge for the result rather than the minutes, so that quicker work doesn't mean smaller pay. You'll learn to spot offers that want your money before you've earned any. Then you'll choose to go ahead, change the idea or stop. Stopping early isn't failure. It means a weak idea cost you a weekend instead of your savings.

By the end, I can't promise you a business. I can say you should have a clear answer about one idea, based on real numbers and real people instead of hopes. Whatever the answer is, you'll know what to do next.

This book is written for people in the UK with a day job and not much spare time. It isn't for building an app, learning to code or hiring a team. It's short enough to read in an evening, and the work fits into a few weekends. Read the chapters in order, because each one builds on the last. You'll need a notebook, a free account with one chat assistant and a willingness to talk to a handful of people.

So take the notebook you've already got open and write down three things you're good at. They can be small. They can be dull. Start there, and turn the page when you're ready.

sections.title: Chapter 1: Start With A Problem, Not A Tool
sections.text:
It's a Tuesday evening, and you're on the sofa with your feet up and your phone in your hand. Someone with very white teeth and very fast speech is telling you that this new AI tool changes everything. You watch the whole video. Then you open three tabs about it, sign up for one free trial and bookmark a list called "27 tools you must try". An hour later you close the phone.

You know more tool names than you did at six o'clock. You have nothing to sell and nothing to test, and you feel further behind than when you sat down. (This is an illustrative scene, but I'd bet it's close to a few of your own evenings.)

## Why The Tool Of The Week Can Wait

Here's the trap. New tools arrive every week, and each one comes with a confident person explaining why you need it. Chasing them feels like progress because it's busy. You read, you click, you compare. But nobody has ever been paid for knowing which tool is newest.

People pay for a problem being solved. That's the whole idea of this chapter, and it's why I ask you to turn the usual order upside down. Pick the problem first. Then choose the plainest tool that helps with it, which is often a free chat assistant and nothing more.

A chat assistant is a program you type to, and it types back. You write a message, called a prompt, such as "give me ten ideas for a birthday party on a small budget", and it replies in seconds with a list. It's quick and tireless, and it never gets bored of your questions. It doesn't know you, your town, your customers or what's worth your time. Treat it like a keen assistant on their first day: useful for drafts and lists, no use for judgement.

So the tool can wait. What you need first is somewhere to point it.

## The Skills You Already Get Paid For

Get your notebook and a pen. Don't open a screen yet.

Write down what you do well at work. Not your job title, but the actual tasks. Do you explain complicated things to nervous people? Do you tidy up other people's messy spreadsheets? Do you know the unwritten rules of your industry, the ones no new starter is told? Then write down what you do well outside work: the friend who plans every holiday, the person everyone asks about allotments, the one who can write a firm but polite complaint letter.

Most people write four or five items and stop. Push to ten. The later items are often the interesting ones, because they're the things you do so easily you've stopped noticing them.

Now look for the overlap. The ideas worth testing usually sit where your own knowledge meets a fiddly task that someone else dislikes. Fiddly means small, repetitive and annoying: formatting, sorting, summarising, explaining, planning. Somebody out there would happily hand it over if it came back done well.

One caution before you go further. If an idea draws on what you know from your day job, read your employment contract first. Some contracts limit outside work or the use of your employer's information. If you're unsure, ask someone qualified to look at it. Better to know now than after you've built something.

## Ten Ideas In Ten Minutes, Then Keep Two

Now open a free chat assistant. Type in your inventory, the whole messy list, and ask for ten small ideas that combine those skills with a fiddly task someone might pay to avoid. Add that you want things one person could make alone, in a weekend, with no coding.

Let me show you how this tends to go, with a composite I'll call Funmi. This is illustrative, not a record of a particular person. Funmi works as a care assistant. In her inventory she wrote that families often ask her the same thing: what should we bring when we visit, and what can we talk about? She asked a chat assistant for ten ideas based on that. Back came a list. Some were sensible. Some were nonsense. Several were the same idea in different clothes.

She threw out eight. They were generic: "an e-book about caring", "a blog for families". The assistant could write those in a minute, and so could anyone else, which is exactly the problem. People rarely pay for something they could get for free in a minute themselves.

She kept two. One was a simple printable visit guide, with ideas for things to bring and things to do together. She asked a colleague about it.

"Would you have used that?"

"Every week."

That's the rhythm to expect. Ten ideas, a bin for most of them, and two that make you think "oh, that's actually something I know about." Notice that the keepers aren't the cleverest ones. They're the ones with your own fingerprints on them: a detail, a setting, a type of person you've actually met. (Funmi's guide, by the way, was about ordinary things like photographs and favourite music. It wasn't medical advice, and it shouldn't be. Anything clinical belongs with qualified professionals.)

If your list looks bland, tell the assistant so. Add more of your own detail and ask again. The sharper your prompt, the less generic the answer.

## Checking Whether Anyone Is Already Asking

Here is the part no tool does for you. An idea you like is still just an idea you like. Before you make anything, look for signs that other people are already asking for help with this problem.

Where? Start close to home. Local community groups on social media are a good place, and so are online forums for your topic. Review sections on books, products and local services are another, because people write exactly what annoyed them. And don't forget the questions customers, colleagues or relatives put to you in ordinary life. If you've been asked the same thing three times, that counts.

Take another illustrative composite, a man I'll call Dan. He works in an office and thought he'd offer AI-written social media posts for small businesses. It seemed obvious. He searched local groups for a week and found nobody asking for it. Plenty of people could write their own posts, and plenty of free tools did it already. He dropped the idea without much pain, which is a fine result for one week of looking.

But while searching, he kept seeing tradespeople in a community group complaining. Their quotes looked messy, they said. Customers were confused by them, and they didn't have time to fix the templates. Dan's day job was full of tidy documents. That complaint became his idea.

Now the harder skill: telling a real signal from a polite nod. A signal sounds like someone with a problem and some urgency. "Does anyone know how to sort this out? I've been putting it off for weeks." A polite nod sounds like "oh, that's a nice idea, you should do it." Nods cost the other person nothing. Signals cost them something: a complaint, a question, a bit of their time, ideally a request for the price. Count the signals. Ignore the nods, however kind they feel.

If you find only silence, that isn't failure. It means you can move to your second idea without having built a thing.

## Your One-line Idea Card

When an idea survives, write it on a single card. An index card works, or a clean page in your notebook. It has four lines.

Who it's for. The problem it solves. What you would hand over. A rough price guess.

Here's Funmi's, filled in as an example:

Who: families visiting a relative in a care setting who aren't sure what to bring or say.
Problem: they feel awkward and unprepared, and visits go quiet.
What I hand over: a two-page printable guide with ideas for things to bring and do together.
Price guess: a few pounds. Only a guess, to be tested.

Keep each line short enough to say out loud to a friend without them blinking. If you can't, the idea is still fuzzy. The price is allowed to be wrong. It's there so the idea is a real offer rather than a daydream, and you'll check it properly later.

Notice what the card doesn't contain: a brand name, a logo, a website or a tool. You haven't needed any of them yet.

### Key Takeaways

- Pick the problem first, then the plainest tool that helps with it.
- The best ideas to test sit where your own knowledge meets a fiddly task someone else dislikes.
- Ask a chat assistant for ten ideas and expect to throw most of them away.
- Look for signals that people are already asking for help, and ignore polite nods.
- Write your idea on one card: who it's for, the problem, what you hand over and a rough price guess.

You now have a card with one small idea on it, and perhaps a few signs that somebody wants it. What you don't have yet is proof, and the quickest way to get some is to put something in front of a handful of people before you spend a weekend, or a subscription, making it pretty.

sections.title: Chapter 2: Test It Before You Build It
sections.text:
Callum spent three weekends on his product. I'll call him that, and the whole scene is illustrative, a composite of how these things tend to go. He'd had an idea for a set of tidy planning templates for people starting a new job. He asked a chat assistant (the program you type to, and it writes back) to draft the contents. He paid for a monthly subscription to a design tool because the free version put a watermark across everything. He chose fonts. He redid the cover twice. By the third Sunday evening it looked lovely, and he finally showed it to a friend, who said, "Oh, that's nice. Who's it for?"

He didn't have a good answer. Nobody had asked for it, and he'd never asked anyone.

Now picture a second person, whom I'll call Helen. She's a bookkeeper with a free Saturday morning and an idea for a monthly receipts tidy-up for sole traders, meaning people who work for themselves without a company. By lunchtime she'd made one sample, written one page and sent five messages to people she knew. She'd spent nothing. By Sunday she knew more than Callum did after three weekends.

## What A Test Is, And What It Is Not

A test is the smallest, cheapest thing you can put in front of real people to find out whether they would pay for what you've in mind. That's all. It answers one question: does anyone want this enough to part with money, or at least to ask what it costs?

A test is not a launch. It isn't a brand, a logo, a website with a clever name or a finished product. Those come later, if they come at all, and you'll be glad you didn't spend a month on them for an idea that turned out to be a polite nod.

Here's the uncomfortable part. Polishing feels like progress. It's comfortable, it's in your control and nobody can say no to a font. Asking five people a plain question feels exposed, which is exactly why it works. If you notice yourself reaching for one more improvement before showing anyone, that's your cue to stop and send a message instead.

## A Lean Kit On Free Plans

You need very little. One chat assistant. One simple way to make a page or a document. One way to take a payment or a pre-order, which is a payment made before the thing exists, on the understanding that you'll deliver later. Three tools, and that's the whole kit.

Start with free plans, the basic no-cost versions of tools, usually with limits on how much you can do. You'll also hear the phrase free tier, which means the same thing. The limits are normally fine for a test. If you hit one, treat it as information rather than a reason to reach for your card.

Pick the plainest option in each category, one you can work out in an evening. Resist trying three assistants side by side. You did enough tool-browsing in Chapter 1, and the point is to get in front of people, not to compare menus.

Before you sign up for anything, set your cap. Decide the most you're willing to spend in a month on this idea, such as £30, and write it on the first line of your notebook. The figure is your choice. It might be £30, £10 or nothing. What matters is that you decide it calmly now, rather than at 10pm when a bright button says "upgrade" and you've had a long day.

Then keep to it. If a tool wants more than the cap, find another or do that step by hand.

## Read The Terms Before You Sell Anything

This is a short section, and I'd like you to take it seriously.

Every tool comes with terms, the long page of rules you tick a box to accept. Some free plans limit commercial use, which means using what the tool makes to earn money. Some restrict exports, meaning how you can save or download your work. The rules differ from tool to tool and they change, so I can't tell you what yours says. Only the maker can.

Here's a small illustrative case. A parent I'll call Joy designs printable meal planners. She'd made a set of pretty illustrations on a free plan and was about to list them for sale. On a whim she read the terms first. The free plan didn't cover commercial use. She switched to a different tool before she'd sold a single thing. It cost her an hour, and it saved her from selling something she wasn't allowed to sell.

So before you sell what a tool produced, find its terms, look for the words "commercial", "personal use" and "export", and read those parts slowly. If anything is unclear, ask the maker through their support page. If real money or a legal question is at stake, take advice from a qualified professional. Who owns AI-made text or images in the UK is also a question I can't settle for you, which is one more reason to check rather than assume. Your day-job contract is worth a glance too, in case it restricts outside work.

## A Sample, A Simple Page And Five Real Conversations

Now the test itself. It has three parts, and you can do all of them in a weekend, or a single morning if your idea is small.

The first is the sample. Make one example of what you'd deliver. Ask your chat assistant for a first draft. A prompt, which is simply the message you type, might be as plain as: "Draft a one-page monthly receipts summary for a self-employed electrician, with headings for materials, fuel and tools." Then do the part the assistant can't. Read it as your buyer would. Fix what's wrong, cut what's padding, add the detail that only someone who knows the work would think of. Use made-up or anonymised details, never a real person's information. The sample should look like something you'd be happy to be judged on, but it doesn't need to be perfect.

The second is a simple page, a single plain page or document that says who the offer is for, what they get, roughly when and what it costs, or that you're still working out the price. Keep it to a few short paragraphs. A word processor and a PDF will do. No colour scheme required.

The third part matters most: five conversations with people who might really want this. Not your mum, unless your mum is your customer. Send a short message, show the sample and ask.

Helen's messages went something like this. She told them she was trying out a monthly receipts tidy-up, attached the sample and asked if she could ask two quick questions. One reply came back within the hour.

"What would it cost me?"

"That is exactly what I'm working out," she wrote. "What would you expect to pay for something like this?"

That exchange tells you more than a dozen compliments. Someone asking the price is someone picturing themselves buying.

Ask questions that don't lead. Avoid "Wouldn't this be useful?" because nearly everyone says yes to be kind. Try these instead:

- How do you handle this at the moment?
- What's the most annoying part of it?
- Have you ever paid anyone, or any tool, to help with it?
- If something like this existed, what would you expect it to cost?

Then stop talking and listen. Write down their actual words in your notebook, not your summary of them. If you're collecting names or contact details, keep it to what you need, store it sensibly and delete it when you're done, as UK data protection rules expect. If anyone offers to pay or pre-order, great, but be clear about what you'd deliver and when, and check the rules on refunds and distance selling on GOV.UK or with Citizens Advice before you take a penny.

## Reading The Results Honestly

When the five conversations are done, sit down with your notebook and be strict with yourself. Hope is very good at reading a shrug as a yes.

Here is the scoring sheet I'd use. It's my own rule of thumb, not a law of nature, so adjust it if your situation is different. Count only what people did or said without being pushed.

A clear yes is when at least two of the five asked the price, asked how to buy or asked when they could have it. Someone describing the problem in their own urgent words, unprompted, also counts. These people have spent something: attention, a question, a little of their time.

A maybe is when people were interested and said it sounded useful, perhaps one asked a question or two, but nobody asked about money. Or the interest was real but aimed at something slightly different from what you showed. Maybes are worth keeping. Write down exactly what each one said, because in the next chapter you'll go back to them.

A no is when the replies were warm but empty ("lovely idea, good luck"), or people already solve this for free, or they shrugged at the problem itself. A no is not an insult. It's the cheapest, fastest answer you could have got, and it cost you a morning.

Be as hard on a yes as on a no. Ask yourself whether you'd bet your own money on it, or only your hopes. Then write one honest line at the bottom of the page: yes, maybe or no, and why. That line, with your notes behind it, is what you carry forward.

### Key Takeaways

- A test is the smallest, cheapest thing you can put in front of real people. It is not a launch, a brand or a finished product.
- Write your monthly spending cap in your notebook before you sign up for any tool.
- Read the terms of every free plan, especially the parts on commercial use and exports, before you sell what it produces.
- One sample, one plain page and five conversations with open questions will teach you more than weeks of polishing.
- Score what people did, not what they were polite enough to say, and sort the result into yes, maybe or no.

You've now got something better than a hope: a page of real answers, some of them probably awkward. What you do with them depends on one question you've so far dodged, which is what a fair price looks like, and why the obvious way of working it out can quietly work against you.

sections.title: Chapter 3: Charge For The Result, Then Decide
sections.text:
You've finished the job. A friend who runs a market stall asked you to sort out her stock list: tidy the columns, fix the prices, make it something she can print and pin up. A year ago that would have eaten your Saturday afternoon. Tonight you gave a chat assistant (the program you type questions to and it writes back) the messy list, checked what it gave you line by line, fixed the three things it got wrong, and you're done in forty minutes.

Now the invoice is open on the screen and your cursor is blinking in the amount box. Forty minutes at your usual hourly rate is a very small number. It feels honest. It also feels like handing over something good for next to nothing.

That small knot in your stomach is worth listening to. It's telling you something about how you've been pricing.

## Why Hourly Pricing Punishes Quick Work

Charging by the hour rewards slowness. The longer the job takes, the more you earn, and the better you get at it, the less you earn. Add an AI tool that takes the fiddly middle out of the work and the sum turns against you twice. The same result now pays a fraction of what it did.

Your friend doesn't care how long it took. She cares that she now has a stock list she can use. The forty minutes is your business, not hers.

There's a second trap, and it catches people who are trying to be kind. Very low prices don't always look like a bargain. Often they look like a warning. If someone offers to tidy your paperwork for the price of a sandwich, a sensible buyer wonders what's wrong with it, or whether the person will turn up. A fair price tells the buyer you take the work seriously, and that you expect them to as well.

None of this means charging whatever you like. It means changing what you're pricing. Stop pricing your minutes and start pricing what the buyer ends up holding.

## Pricing The Result In Three Steps

Here's the method, in three plain steps. Do them with your notebook open and your idea card from Chapter 1 beside you.

First, describe the result in one sentence, from the buyer's side. Not "I will format a spreadsheet." Instead: "You get a clean, printable stock list with correct prices, ready by Friday." If you can't say what the buyer ends up with, the offer is still fuzzy, and a fuzzy offer is hard to price.

Second, ask what that result saves or brings them, in their words rather than yours. Your friend might say it saves her a Sunday evening she'd rather spend with her family. Another buyer might say it stops customers asking the same question forty times a day. Another might say it means fewer mistakes at the till. You don't need a spreadsheet of calculations. You need one honest answer to "what is this worth to you?", and the ability to hear it. You already asked what people would expect to pay in your Chapter 2 conversations, so look back at what they said.

Third, set a project price you can explain in one sentence. "It's £60 for the finished list, including one round of changes." That's a sentence a buyer can repeat to someone else. If your explanation needs three clauses and an apology, the price isn't ready yet.

Then package it as a fixed offer. Say what's included, how many changes are covered, and when it will be delivered. A clear box with a clear price is easier to say yes to than an open-ended favour.

Let me tell you about someone, and this is an illustrative story, not a record of one particular person. I'll call him Peter. He's a retired teacher who offered to tidy lesson resources for private tutors: scruffy worksheets, mismatched fonts, answer sheets in the wrong order. With a chat assistant doing the first pass and Peter doing the checking, a term's worth took him around three hours. His first instinct was to quote by the hour, and the total looked embarrassingly small. He nearly gave the work away.

Then he rewrote the offer. "A tidy, ready-to-print pack for your term's lessons, with one round of changes, for a fixed price." He chose the price after asking two tutors what a clear pack would save them over a term. His first buyer found it easier to say yes, because she knew what she was getting and what it would cost, and she didn't have to wonder how many hours it might turn into.

Now, a firm word of caution. A price you reach this way is a starting point for your own judgement. It is not a promise of what anyone will pay. So test it. Go back to the people who said maybe in Chapter 2, the ones who liked the idea but never asked about money. Send them the fixed offer with the price in it and ask plainly whether it sounds fair. Their reaction, whether a question, a hesitation or a counter-offer, is more useful than any figure I could give you. If you're selling to individual customers rather than other businesses, GOV.UK and Citizens Advice both explain refund rights, so read them before you take a penny.

## Spotting Offers That Want Your Money First

While you're working on your own small test, other offers will find you. You may already have had one.

Here's another illustrative scene. A message arrives from someone friendly, who has seen your name somewhere and thinks you'd be perfect for a "ready-made AI business." Everything is done for you. The site is built, the system is running. All that's needed is a starter fee, and the offer closes tonight.

Look at how that's shaped. You're being asked to pay before you've earned anything. It leans on a deadline. It's vague about who is behind it and how the money would actually reach you. And it makes things sound effortless, which is the opposite of what you've seen so far in this book. Testing an idea has been small, a bit awkward and full of conversations.

The person in my scene read the message twice, noticed those signs, declined and went back to the sample and the five conversations they already had. It cost them nothing, and that is the point.

So the warning signs are these. Be wary of any offer that asks for money before you can earn, that promises easy or certain results, that pushes you to decide quickly, that won't say clearly who runs it, or that makes its money by getting you to recruit others. Before you hand over anything, check the Financial Conduct Authority's warning list and its guidance on scams, and look at what Citizens Advice and GOV.UK say about the kind of offer you're considering. If you're unsure, talk to someone you trust, or to a qualified adviser, before you pay. A genuine opportunity will still be there after a night's sleep.

## Go, Change Or Stop

Take out your scoring sheet from Chapter 2. You sorted your results into clear yes, maybe and no. Now that sheet makes the decision for you, with a bit of your own sense on top.

Go means at least two people asked about price or delivery, and your priced offer didn't scare them off. Someone has pictured themselves buying. That's enough to carry on, with small steps.

Change means you got interest without anyone reaching for their wallet. Don't abandon the idea and don't charge ahead. Pick one thing to alter: who it's for, which problem you're solving, or what you hand over. Then test again. Most ideas that survive do so after one change.

Stop means the replies were kind and empty. Nobody asked what it cost, nobody asked when they could have it, and your price didn't land. Stopping is allowed. In fact, I'd go further and call it a result.

Think about what happened. You spent a weekend, perhaps a few evenings, and nothing you couldn't afford. In exchange you learned that this idea wasn't going to work, before you bought equipment or signed up for a subscription, and before you told your family you were starting a business. Weigh that against someone who finds out the same thing after months and a chunk of their savings. Your answer arrived early and cheap. That's the method working.

## Your Next Thirty Days

Whichever you chose, give the next thirty days a shape, and give each week a time limit. Set it before you begin, write it in your notebook, and keep to it. The point is to protect your day job and your evenings. Check your employment contract too, in case it limits outside work, and look at GOV.UK's guidance on declaring any income you do start to earn.

If you chose go, allow about three hours a week. In week one, write the fixed offer and price on a single page and send it to the people who showed interest. In week two, deliver the first job, or take a first pre-order (a payment made before the thing exists, on the understanding you'll deliver later). In week three, ask your first buyer what worked and what didn't, and note how long the job really took. In week four, look at your notes and decide whether to carry on at the same pace.

If you chose change, two hours a week is plenty. Week one is for choosing the one thing to change and writing down why. Week two, rework the sample and the page. Week three, take it to five people, some from your maybes and some new. Week four, score it again, honestly, and choose again.

If you chose stop, one hour a week will do. Week one, write down what you learned and file the card where you can find it. Week two, rest. Weeks three and four, go back to Chapter 1, ask a chat assistant for ten new ideas and fill in a fresh card. The skills you listed are still yours.

Notice that none of these plans asks for a late night or a spending spree. They ask for a few steady hours, and an honest look at the result at the end.

### Key Takeaways

- Charging by the hour means faster work earns you less, and very low prices can make buyers doubt you.
- Price the result: say what the buyer gets, what it saves or brings them, and set a price you can explain in one sentence.
- Test your price with your maybes from Chapter 2, and treat it as a starting point, not a promise.
- Be wary of any offer that asks for money before you can earn, and check official UK guidance first.
- Stopping a weak idea early is a good result. Whatever you choose, give the next thirty days a weekly time limit.

You now have a price, a decision and a plan that fits around your life. Something else is sitting in your notebook as well: a method you've used once, which means you can use it again. The next question is what to do with that.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.text:
# Small Is How It Starts

Go back to that kitchen table for a moment. Same chair, same weeknight, probably a fresh cup of tea going cold beside you. The notebook looks different now. Where there was a blank page, there's an idea card, a scoring sheet, a price you can say in one sentence and a decision with a date next to it. Whether that decision was go, change or stop, it's yours, and it came from real people rather than from hope.

That's the whole method, and it's smaller than it sounded when we started. Pick a problem before a tool. Test before you build. Price the result, then decide. None of it depended on a particular product, which is why it'll still work when the tools on your phone have all been replaced.

Here's what I'd like you to notice. You can do it again. Every idea gets its own card, its own test and its own decision. Illustrative example: Sam works in a warehouse office and stopped his first idea after five polite, empty conversations. It cost him one Saturday. His second card came from a question colleagues kept asking him about shift rotas, and the second test drew two people asking the price. Same notebook, same loop, different answer.

A test that keeps saying yes can grow slowly. It might become a small, repeatable offer you deliver to a few people. It might become a digital product, which just means something you make once and can sell more than once. Neither has to happen quickly, and neither is promised. Some ideas will stay small, and that's allowed.

Protect the time limits you set in Chapter 3. They're what keep a side business a side business. If the hours creep up, write the number down and ask whether that's a choice or a drift. Check your employment contract for anything about outside work, and look at the official guidance on declaring extra income before it becomes more than pocket money. Those are ten-minute jobs now and awkward ones later.

Tools will keep changing, and people will keep telling you that you're behind. You're not. The plainest tool that does the job is enough, and the part that matters most has never been automated: asking someone a straight question and listening to the answer.

I can't tell you your idea will work. I can tell you that you now have a way to find out cheaply, quickly and without lying to yourself, and that's worth more than most of what's being sold out there.

So here's your step for this week. Open the notebook to the first clean page. Write one small next step at the top, the sort you can finish in under an hour. Maybe it's sending the message you've been putting off, or starting a second card. Then put a time next to it, and keep that time.

Small is how it starts. Go and start.

sections.title: A small request
sections.text: If this book helped you test an idea more calmly, I would be grateful if you would leave an honest review on the store where you bought it. Reviews help other readers find the book and decide whether it is right for them. Thank you for reading, and for choosing small steps.
